content: Macaroni and cheese, a dish popular in regions such as Canada and the British Isles, is a culinary preparation that closely resembles the British dish known as cauliflower cheese. Its primary components include cooked macaroni pasta, often referred to as elbow macaroni in the United States, and a cheese-based sauce. Traditionally, cheddar cheese or processed cheese with a cheddar-like flavor is used, although other types of cheese may also be incorporated. Packaged versions of macaroni and cheese are widely available and typically consist of boxed pasta accompanied by a powdered cheese mix. To prepare these, one adds butter and milk (or water) to the mix. Additional ingredients, such as ground beef, canned tuna, ketchup, sliced hot dogs, ham, bacon, peppers, tomatoes, or other vegetables, are sometimes included to enhance the dish. However, purists may argue that such variations deviate from the essence of macaroni and cheese. When prepared using traditional methods, the cheese sauce is often made in the style of a Mornay sauce, a classic French culinary preparation. This involves creating a roux by cooking butter and flour together, to which milk and cheese are subsequently added. Alternatively, the sauce may be based on a custard mixture with cheese incorporated. The cheese sauce is then combined with the cooked macaroni. In many cases, the dish is baked as a casserole, often topped with breadcrumbs. This baking process creates a textural contrast between the soft interior and the crisp exterior, achieved through dry-heat cooking. A stovetop version of macaroni and cheese involves slowly melting the cheese over heat to integrate it with the cooked pasta. In this method, the sauce is prepared in the same pan, with other ingredients mixed separately. Boxed stovetop versions of macaroni and cheese have been available since 1937. These versions are characterized by their vibrant yellow-orange color, which is derived from the powdered cheese sauce mix rather than actual cheese. This distinctive color was immortalized in 1993 when Crayola introduced a macaroni and cheese crayon to their collection, named by a six-year-old contest winner, Jason Riggs. In Canada, boxed macaroni and cheese is commonly referred to as Kraft Dinner, reflecting the dominance of Kraft Foods' product in the region. Anecdotal accounts suggest that macaroni and cheese was invented by Thomas Jefferson. According to a version of the story shared by Alton Brown of Good Eats, Jefferson, unable to procure an Italian pasta-making machine, designed his own device, produced macaroni, and instructed his cook to bake it with generous amounts of York cheddar cheese, creating a casserole. Food writer Jeffrey Steingarten describes an 1802 recipe as the very first recipe ever printed on the back of an American box. While not technically printed on a box, the recipe was included on sheets of paper wrapped around bundles of dried vermicelli and macaroni produced in Philadelphia by Lewis Fresnaye. The historic recipe reads as follows: Take six pints of water and boil it with a sufficient amount of salt. When boiling, stir in one pound of pasta and let it cook. Then strain the water thoroughly and place the pasta in a large dish, mixing it with six ounces of grated Parmesan or other good cheese. Next, take four ounces of good butter, melt it well in a small pot or saucer, and pour it over the pasta while both are still warm. For an improved result, place the dish in a hot oven for a few minutes until the butter and cheese have thoroughly penetrated the pasta. The dish can be made even more delicate by boiling the pasta in milk instead of water and adding a little meat gravy or any other meat sauce on top.
